{{Short description|Pedagogy emphasizing problem-solving mastery}}
'''Singapore math''' (or '''Singapore maths''' in [[British English]]<ref name="The Independent">{{cite news|author= The Independent|title=Box clever: Singapore's magic formula for maths success|newspaper=The Independent|date=July 2, 2009|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/education/schools/box-clever-singapores-magic-formula-for-maths-success-1727053.html}}</ref>) is a teaching method based on the national mathematics curriculum used for first through sixth grade in Singaporean schools.<ref name="Laura Brown">{{cite web
 | last = Brown | first =Laura L. | title = What's Singapore Math?| publisher = PBS | access-date=September 19, 2013| url=https://www.pbs.org/parents/education/math/math-tips-for-parents/whats-singapore-math/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120710081119/http://www.pbs.org/parents/education/math/math-tips-for-parents/whats-singapore-math/ | url-status=dead | archive-date=July 10, 2012 }}</ref><ref name="Winnie Hu">{{cite news |last=Hu| first= Winnie| title=Making Math Lessons as Easy as 1, Pause, 2, Pause&nbsp;... |newspaper=The New York Times| location= New York, NY |date= September 30, 2010 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/10/01/education/01math.html}}</ref> The term was coined in the [[United States]]<ref name="US term">{{cite web | last = Jackson | first = Bill | title = Going Beyond Singapore Math: Resisting Quick Fixes | publisher = Singapore Math Source | date = July 26, 2011 | url = http://singaporemathsource.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/02/Resisting-Quick-Fixes.pdf | access-date = July 19, 2014 }}</ref> to describe an approach originally developed in Singapore to teach students to learn and master fewer mathematical concepts at greater detail as well as having them learn these concepts using a three-step learning process: concrete, pictorial, and abstract.<ref name="Laura Brown" /><ref name="Winnie Hu" /> In the concrete step, students engage in hands-on learning experiences using physical objects which can be everyday items such as paper clips, toy blocks or math manipulates such as counting bears, link cubes and fraction discs.<ref name="Lindsay Knake">{{cite news | last=Knake |first= Lindsay | title= Saginaw Township elementary schools implement hands-on Singapore math program| newspaper= MLive |location= Grand Rapids, MI |date= December 2011 |url=http://www.mlive.com/news/saginaw/index.ssf/2011/12/saginaw_township_elementary_sc.html}}</ref> This is followed by drawing pictorial representations of mathematical concepts. Students then solve mathematical problems in an abstract way by using numbers and symbols.<ref name="Bill Jackson">{{cite news|last=Jackson|first= Bill| title=My view: America's students can benefit from Singapore math|newspaper=CNN| location=Atlanta, GA| date=October 10, 2012|url=http://schoolsofthought.blogs.cnn.com/2012/10/10/my-view-americas-students-can-benefit-from-singapore-math/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121013035331/http://schoolsofthought.blogs.cnn.com/2012/10/10/my-view-americas-students-can-benefit-from-singapore-math/|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 13, 2012}}</ref>

The development of Singapore math began in the 1980s when [[Singapore]]'s [[Ministry of Education (Singapore)|Ministry of Education]] developed its own mathematics textbooks that focused on problem solving and developing thinking skills.<ref name="Winnie Hu" /><ref name="Gerard Wright">{{cite news | last=Wright|first= Gerard| title=Mathematics Mighty Ducks| newspaper=The Age|location= Australia|date = May 12, 2008 |url=http://www.theage.com.au/news/education-news/mathematics-mighty-ducks/2008/05/10/1210131279908.html}}</ref> Outside Singapore, these textbooks were adopted by several schools in the [[United States]] and in other countries such as [[Canada]], [[Israel]], the [[Netherlands]], [[Indonesia]], [[Chile]], [[Jordan]], [[India]], [[Pakistan]], [[Thailand]], [[Malaysia]], [[Japan]], [[South Korea]], the [[Philippines]] and the [[United Kingdom]].<ref name="The Independent"/><ref name="Cris Prystay">{{cite news|last=Prystay|first=Cris|title=As math skills slip, U.S. schools seek answers from Asia|newspaper=The Wall Street Journal|date=December 13, 2004|url=https://online.wsj.com/news/articles/SB110288916514797758}}</ref><ref name=Wong>{{cite book|last1=Wong|first1=Khoon Yoong|last2=Lee|first2=Ngan Hoe|chapter=Singapore education and mathematics curriculum |title=Mathematics Education: The Singapore Journey| editor=Wong Koon Yoong|editor2=Lee Peng Yee|editor3=Berinderjeet Kaur| editor4=Foong Pui Yee |editor5=Ng Swee Fong|volume=2|date=February 19, 2009|publisher=World Scientific Publishing|pages=13–47|location=Singapore |isbn=978-981-283-375-4}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.smartparenting.com.ph/parenting/preschooler/mathemagis-introducing-singapore-math-in-the-philippines|title=Mathemagis: Introducing Singapore Math in the Philippines|date=2012-04-12|website=SmartParenting.com.ph|access-date=2019-09-27}}</ref> Early adopters of these textbooks in the U.S. included parents interested in [[homeschooling]] as well as a limited number of schools.<ref name="Winnie Hu" /> These textbooks became more popular since the release of scores from international education surveys such as [[Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study]] (TIMSS) and [[Programme for International Student Assessment]] (PISA), which showed Singapore at the top three of the world since 1995.<ref name="Garelick Barry">{{cite journal | last = Garelick | first = Barry | title = Miracle math: A successful program from Singapore tests the limits of school reform in the suburbs. | journal = Education Next | volume=6 | date = Fall 2006 | url = http://educationnext.org/miracle-math/}}</ref><ref name="timss2015"/> U.S. editions of these textbooks have since been adopted by a large number of [[School district#United States|school districts]] as well as [[Charter schools in the United States|charter]] and [[private schools]].<ref name="Winnie Hu" />

== History ==

Before the development of its own mathematics textbooks in the 1980s, Singapore imported its mathematics textbooks from other countries.<ref name="Peng Yee Lee">{{cite conference|last=Lee|first=Peng Yee|title=Sixty years of mathematics syllabi and textbooks in Singapore|book-title=Mathematics Curriculum in Pacific Rim Countries—China, Japan, Korea, and Singapore Proceedings of a Conference|editor-last=Usiskin|editor-first=Zalman |editor2-last=Willmore |editor2-first=Edwin|pages=85–92|publisher=Information Age Publishing |date=September 12, 2008|isbn=978-1-59311-953-9 }}</ref> In 1981, the Curriculum Development Institute of Singapore (CDIS) (currently the Curriculum Planning and Development Division) began to develop its own mathematics textbooks and curriculum. The CDIS developed and distributed a textbook series for [[Primary school|elementary schools]] in Singapore called ''Primary Mathematics'', which was first published in 1982 and subsequently revised in 1992 to emphasize problem solving.<ref name="Garelick Barry2">{{cite journal | last = Garelick | first = Barry | title = A tale of two countries and one school district. | journal = Nonpartisan Education Review | volume = 6 | issue = 8 | year = 2006 | url = http://npe.educationnews.org/Review/Essays/v2n8.htm | access-date = 2013-09-20 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130921060409/http://npe.educationnews.org/Review/Essays/v2n8.htm | archive-date = 2013-09-21 | url-status = dead }}</ref><ref name=fang>{{cite book|last1=Fang|first1=Yanping|last2=Lee|first2=Christine Kim-Eng|last3=Haron|first3=Sharifah Thalha Bte Syed|chapter=Lesson study in mathematics: Three cases in Singapore |title=Mathematics Education: The Singapore Journey| editor=Wong Koon Yoong|editor2=Lee Peng Yee|editor3=Berinderjeet Kaur| editor4=Foong Pui Yee |editor5=Ng Swee Fong|volume=2|date=February 19, 2009|publisher=World Scientific Publishing|pages=104–129|location=Singapore |isbn=978-981-283-375-4}}</ref> In the late 1990s, the country's Ministry of Education opened the elementary school textbook market to private companies, and [[Marshall Cavendish]],  a local and private publisher of educational materials, began to publish and market the ''Primary Mathematics'' textbooks.<ref name="The Independent" /><ref name=fang/><ref name="Mitchell Landsberg">{{cite news|last=Landsberg|first=Mitchell|title=In L.A., Singapore math has added value|newspaper=Los Angeles Times|location=Los Angeles, CA|date=March 9, 2008|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2008-mar-09-me-math9-story.html}}</ref>

Following Singapore's curricular and instructional initiatives, dramatic improvements in math proficiency among Singaporean students on international assessments were observed.<ref name="The Independent"/> TIMSS, an international assessment for math and science among fourth and eighth graders, ranked Singapore's fourth and eighth grade students first in mathematics four times (1995, 1999, 2003, and 2015) among participating nations.<ref name="Garelick Barry"/><ref name="Garelick Barry2"/><ref name="timss2015">{{cite news|last=Gurney-Read|first=Josie|title=Revealed: World pupil rankings in science and maths - TIMSS results in full|newspaper=The Daily Telegraph|date=November 29, 2016|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/education/2016/11/29/revealed-world-pupil-rankings-science-maths-timss-results/}}</ref> Likewise, the [[Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development]] (OECD)'s [[Programme for International Student Assessment]] (PISA), a worldwide study of 15-year-old school students' scholastic performance in mathematics, [[science]], and [[Reading (process)|reading]], has ranked Singaporean students first in 2015,<ref name="pisa2015">{{cite news|last=Coughlan|first=Sean|title=Pisa tests: Singapore top in global education rankings|publisher=BBC|date=December 6, 2016|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/education-38212070}}</ref> and second after [[Shanghai]], [[China]] in 2009 and 2012.<ref name=dillon>{{cite news|last=Dillon|first=sam|title=Top test scores from shanghai stun educators|newspaper=New York Times|location=New York, NY|date=December 7, 2010|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/12/07/education/07education.html?pagewanted=all}}</ref><ref name=economist>{{cite news|author=The Economist|title=Finn-ished|newspaper=The Economist|date=December 7, 2013|url=https://www.economist.com/news/international/21591195-fall-former-nordic-education-star-latest-pisa-tests-focusing-interest}}</ref>

Since the TIMSS publication of Singapore's high ranking in mathematics, professional mathematicians in the U.S. took a closer look at Singapore mathematics textbooks such as ''Primary Mathematics''.<ref name="Garelick Barry"/> The term ''Singapore math'' was originally coined in the U.S. to describe the teaching approach based on these textbooks.<ref name="US term" /> In 2005, the [[American Institutes for Research]] (AIR) published a study, which concluded that U.S. schools could benefit from adopting these textbooks.<ref name="Garelick Barry"/> The textbooks were already distributed in the U.S. by Singapore Math, Inc., a private venture based in Oregon.<ref name="Garelick Barry2"/> Early users of these textbooks in the U.S. included parents interested in [[homeschooling]] as well as a limited number of schools.<ref name="Winnie Hu" /> They became more popular since the release of the TIMSS scores showing Singapore's top ranking.<ref name="Garelick Barry"/> As of 2004, U.S. versions of Singapore mathematics textbooks were adopted in over 200 U.S. schools.<ref name="Winnie Hu" /><ref name="Cris Prystay" /> Schools and counties that had adopted these textbooks reported improvements in their students' performance.<ref name="Cris Prystay"/><ref name="Garelick Barry"/><ref name="Mitchell Landsberg" /><ref name="Kyle Moroney">{{cite news|last=Moroney|first=Kyle|title=How Common Core standards are affecting elementary, middle school math classes|newspaper=MLive|date=December 2, 2013|url=http://www.mlive.com/news/grand-rapids/index.ssf/2013/12/kentwood_first_west_michigan_s.html}}</ref> Singapore math textbooks were also used in schools from other countries such as [[Canada]], [[Israel]], [[the Philippines]] and the [[United Kingdom]].<ref name="The Independent"/><ref name="Cris Prystay"/><ref name=Wong/>

==Features==

===Covers fewer topics in greater depth===

Compared to a traditional U.S. math curriculum, Singapore math focuses on fewer topics but covers them in greater detail.<ref name="Winnie Hu" /> Each semester-level Singapore math textbook builds upon prior knowledge and skills, with students mastering them before moving on to the next grade. Students, therefore, need not re-learn these skills at the next grade level.<ref name="Laura Brown"/> By the end of sixth grade, Singapore math students have mastered multiplication and division of fractions and can solve difficult multi-step word problems.<ref name="Hoven and Garelick">{{cite journal | last1 = Hoven | first1 = John | last2 = Garelick | first2 = Barry | title = Singapore Math: Using the bar model approach, Singapore textbooks enable students to solve difficult math problems--and learn how to think symbolically. | journal = Educational Leadership | volume = 65 | pages = 28–21 | date = November 2007 | url = http://www.utahsmathfuture.com/usj.pdf | access-date = 2013-09-20 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20131019223239/http://utahsmathfuture.com/usj.pdf | archive-date = 2013-10-19 | url-status = usurped }}</ref>

In the U.S., it was found that Singapore math emphasizes the essential math skills recommended in the 2006 Focal Points publication by the [[National Council of Teachers of Mathematics]] (NCTM), the 2008 final report by the National Mathematics Advisory Panel, and the proposed [[Common Core State Standards Initiative|Common Core State Standards]], though it generally progresses to topics at an earlier grade level compared to U.S. standards.<ref name="www2.ed.gov">{{cite web|author=National Mathematics Advisory Panel |title=Foundations for Success: The Final Report of the National Mathematics Advisory Panel|url=http://www2.ed.gov/about/bdscomm/list/mathpanel/report/final-report.pdf | publisher=U.S. Department of Education| date=March 2008|access-date=December 13, 2013}}</ref><ref name="Sarah Garland">{{cite news |last=Garland|first= Sarah|title=How Does Common Core Compare?|newspaper= Huffington Post|date= October 16, 2013|url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2013/10/15/common-core-compare_n_4102973.html }}</ref>

===Three-step learning process===

{{Main|Arithmetic}}
[[File:Whole-part model addition 70 plus 30.jpg|thumb|right|250px| A bar model used to solve an addition problem. This pictorial approach is typically used as a problem-solving tool in Singapore math.]]
Singapore math teaches students mathematical concepts in a three-step learning process: concrete, pictorial, and abstract.<ref name="Winnie Hu"/> This learning process was based on the work of an American psychologist, [[Jerome Bruner]]. In the 1960s, Bruner found that people learn in three stages by first handling real objects before transitioning to pictures and then to symbols.<ref name="BBC">{{cite web|author=BBC|title=Can the Singapore method help your children learn maths?|publisher=BBC|date=December 2, 2013|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/skillswise/0/24925787|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203191611/http://www.bbc.co.uk/skillswise/0/24925787|url-status=dead|archive-date=December 3, 2013}}</ref> The Singapore government later adapted this approach to their math curriculum in the 1980s.

The first of the three steps is concrete, wherein students learn while handling objects such as chips, dice, or paper clips.<ref name="Lindsay Knake" /> Students learn to count these objects (e.g., paper clips) by physically lining them up in a row. They then learn basic [[Arithmetic#Arithmetic operations|arithmetic operations]] such as [[addition]] or [[subtraction]] by physically adding or removing the objects from each row.<ref name="BBC" />

Students then transition to the pictorial step by drawing diagrams called "bar-models" to represent specific quantities of an object.<ref name="Garelick Barry" /><ref name="BBC" /> This involves drawing a rectangular bar to represent a specific quantity. For instance, if a short bar represents five paper clips, a bar that is twice as long would represent ten. By visualizing the difference between the two bars, students learn to solve problems of addition by adding one bar to the other, which will, in this instance, produce an answer of fifteen paper clips. They can use this method to solve other mathematical problems involving subtraction, [[multiplication]], and [[Division (mathematics)|division]].<ref name="Garelick Barry" /><ref name="Hoven and Garelick" /> Bar modeling is far more efficient than the "guess-and-check" approach, in which students simply guess combinations of numbers until they stumble onto the solution.<ref name="Garelick Barry" />

Once students have learned to solve mathematical problems using bar modeling, they begin to solve mathematical problems with exclusively abstract tools: numbers and symbols.

[[File:whole-part model multiplication.jpg|thumb|right|250px| The whole-part model can also be used to solve a multiplication problem.]]

===Bar modeling===

Bar modeling is a pictorial method used to solve [[Word problem (mathematics education)|word problems]] in [[arithmetic]].<ref name="Hoven and Garelick" /><ref name="Frank Shaffer">{{cite book | author=Frank Schaffer Publications|chapter=Introduction to Singapore Math|title=70 Must-Know Word Problems, Grade 7 (Singapore Math) |date=June 2009| pages=3–8|publisher=Frank Schaffer Publications|edition=workbook|isbn=978-0-7682-4016-0}}</ref> These bar models can come in multiple forms such as a whole-part or a comparison model.

With the whole-part model, students would draw a rectangular bar to represent a "whole" larger quantity, which can be subdivided into two or more "parts." A student could be exposed to a word problem involving addition such as:

:''If John has 70 apples and Jane has 30 apples, how many apples do they both have?''

The solution to this problem could be solved by drawing one bar  and dividing it into two parts, with the longer part as 70 and the shorter part as 30. By visualizing these two parts, students would simply solve the above word problem by adding both parts together to build a whole bar of 100. Conversely, a student could use whole-part model to solve a subtraction problem such as 100 - 70, by having the longer part be 70 and the whole bar be 100. They would then solve the problem by inferring the shorter part to be 30.

[[File:Comparison model subtraction.jpg|thumb|right|250px| The bar model can be drawn as a comparison model to compare two bars of unequal lengths, which can then be used to solve a subtraction problem.]]

The whole-part model can also be used to solve problems involving multiplication or division.<ref name=Jackson2>{{cite web|last=Jackson|first=Bill|title=Singapore math bar model strategy|url=http://www.thedailyriff.com/WordProblems.pdf|access-date=December 16, 2013 |publisher=The Daily Riff}}</ref> A multiplication problem could be presented as follows:

:''How much money would Jane have if she saved $30 each week for 4 weeks in a row?''

The student could solve this multiplication problem by drawing one bar to represent the unknown answer, and subdivide that bar into four equal parts, with each part representing $30.  Based on the drawn model, the student could then visualize this problem as providing a solution of $120.

Unlike the whole-part model, a comparison model involves comparing two bars of unequal lengths.<ref name="Hoven and Garelick" /><ref name="Frank Shaffer" /> It can be used to solve a subtraction problem such as the following:

:''John needs to walk 100 miles to reach his home. So far, he has walked 70 miles. How many miles does he have left to walk home?''

By using the comparison model, the student would draw one long bar to represent 100 and another shorter bar to represent 70. By comparing these two bars, students could then solve for the difference between the two numbers, which in this case is 30 miles. Like the whole-part model, the comparison model can also be used to solve word problems involving addition, multiplication, and division.
